pentecostal.holy_spirit:
Pentecostals confess the Holy Spirit as the third person of the Trinity, fully God, and as a living presence who is active in the church and in the lives of believers today. The Spirit convicts of sin, brings new birth, dwells in every believer from conversion, and guides and empowers God's people for holy living and witness.

What marks Pentecostal teaching is the emphasis on knowing the Spirit by experience and not only by doctrine. Worship expects that the Holy Spirit will move among the congregation, healing, speaking and giving gifts as he wills. Pentecostals use both Holy Spirit and Holy Ghost, and they draw their expectation from the events of Pentecost in the Acts of the Apostles, which they regard as a pattern for the whole of church history.
pentecostal.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Pentecostals believe that the Holy Spirit still gives spiritual gifts to believers for the building up of the church. They often speak of nine gifts, following the list in the First Letter to the Corinthians: a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, different kinds of tongues and the interpretation of tongues.

The gifts are understood as given by the Spirit as he chooses, not earned, and their purpose is to serve others and to strengthen the church. Pentecostals also teach that gifts should be exercised in an orderly manner, weighed against Scripture, and used with love, following the same letter's instructions. Many congregations make room in services for these gifts, and members are encouraged to seek them.
pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Most Pentecostals teach that baptism in the Holy Spirit, also called Spirit baptism or the infilling of the Spirit, is an experience distinct from and following conversion, in which the believer is filled with the Holy Spirit and empowered for witness and service. They base this on the accounts in the Acts of the Apostles and on the promise of Jesus that his followers would receive power.

Many classical Pentecostal bodies teach that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence that a person has received it. Believers are encouraged to seek this experience by asking in faith. Some Holiness Pentecostal groups describe it as a third work following conversion and sanctification. Pentecostals do not regard it as a requirement for salvation, but as an additional gift which God intends for every believer.
pentecostal.tongues:
Pentecostals speak in tongues, also called glossolalia: speaking words that the speaker has not learned, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. In personal prayer it is understood as a spiritual language for praise and intercession. In the congregation, a message in tongues is to be followed by an interpretation, so that the church is built up.

Many Pentecostal denominations teach that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit, drawing on the accounts in Acts. Not every Pentecostal body holds it in the same way, and some see tongues as one of several possible signs. Pentecostals do not regard it as a requirement for salvation, and they teach that the gift, like the others, must be used in order and in love.
pentecostal.continuationism:
Pentecostals hold that the spiritual gifts and signs found in the New Testament, including healing, prophecy and tongues, have not ceased and remain available to the church today. They do not find in Scripture any statement that these gifts would end before Christ returns, and they read the passage about gifts passing away as referring to the return of Christ.

They also point to the history of the church and to the testimony of believers around the world who report experiences of the Spirit's power. The gifts are to be tested against Scripture, and Scripture remains the final authority. Christians who hold that the sign gifts ceased with the apostolic age disagree, and Pentecostals see this as one of the major differences between themselves and cessationist churches.
pentecostal.continuing_revelation:
Pentecostals believe in prophecy as a gift of the Holy Spirit that continues in the church today. In the Pentecostal view, prophecy means a word from God given through a believer to encourage, strengthen and comfort others, as described in the First Letter to the Corinthians.

They do not understand such words as adding to Scripture. The Bible is complete and is the standard by which every prophetic word is tested, and the congregation or its leaders are expected to weigh what is said. A prophecy that contradicts Scripture is rejected. Pentecostals distinguish the ordinary gift of prophecy from the work of the biblical prophets who wrote Scripture, and they hold that God still speaks to and through his people today.
pentecostal.prophetic_authority:
Some Pentecostal and charismatic groups recognize prophets as a ministry office, referring to the list of ministries given to the church in the Letter to the Ephesians. Such a person is understood to have a recurring gift of prophecy and to serve the church by speaking what the Spirit gives.

Views and practice differ considerably. Many classical Pentecostal denominations speak mainly of the gift of prophecy exercised by any believer, and do not give a formal office of prophet special authority. Where prophets are recognized, their words are to be tested against Scripture and judged by the local church. No Pentecostal body holds that a prophet's words carry authority equal to the Bible, and pastors and elders remain responsible for the oversight of the church.
pentecostal.apostles_today:
Pentecostals often speak of the fivefold ministry listed in the Letter to the Ephesians: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. Some Pentecostal networks and many newer charismatic movements believe that God still calls apostles today, as church planters, founders of movements or overseers of many churches.

Other Pentecostals do not use the title, and many of the historic denominations do not recognize apostles in the sense of the original Twelve. When the word is used, it usually does not mean that a modern apostle has authority equal to the first apostles or can add to Scripture. Practice differs widely, and people who hold the title are expected to submit to Scripture and to the accountability of a wider body of church leaders.
pentecostal.anointing_of_the_sick:
Pentecostals pray for the sick and follow the instruction in the Letter of James that a person who is ill should call for the elders of the church, who anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord and pray in faith. The oil is a symbol of the Holy Spirit and is not thought to have power in itself.

Pentecostals believe that God heals today, and that healing was provided through Christ's suffering. Prayer for healing is a regular part of many services, often with the laying on of hands. They recognize that God heals in his own way and time, and not everyone who is prayed for is healed. Most Pentecostals also use doctors and medicine, and see medicine and prayer as working together.
pentecostal.altar_call:
In many Pentecostal churches the sermon ends with an altar call, an invitation for people to come forward to the front of the sanctuary to pray. The front is called the altar, not because a sacrifice is offered but because it is a place of prayer and commitment. Those who come may be receiving Christ for the first time, returning to faith, seeking healing or asking to be filled with the Spirit.

The altar call gives people a chance to respond publicly and immediately to what has been preached, and members often gather around to pray with them. It reflects the Pentecostal expectation that God acts in the present moment. It is not thought to be required for salvation, and where the service leaves plenty of time for prayer, the altar time can be a central part of worship.
